item.title: Information ethics education and artificial intelligence ethical judgment among university students
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become an everyday study tool for university students, and how students judge its acceptable academic use is now an explicit target of educational policy. This cluster-randomized experiment tested whether an information ethics education module improves university students’ AI ethical judgment, whether improvements persist over four weeks, and whether effects depend on students’ daily generative AI use. Sixteen intact classes from three universities in Zhengzhou, China, were randomly assigned at the class level to a four-week information ethics education module (eight classes, n = 120) or to regular coursework (eight classes, n = 120). AI ethical judgment was measured before the module, immediately afterward, and four weeks later with a double-rated dilemma test covering six academic scenarios and three dimensions (ethical sensitivity, evaluative judgment, behavioral intention); inter-rater ICC(2,1) values were 0.897, 0.923, and 0.930 at the three waves. The design-consistent primary analysis, a multilevel model with random intercepts for students and classes, yielded a significant arm by wave interaction, χ 2 (2) = 60.94, p < 0.001: composite judgment rose in the intervention arm and did not change in the control arm. Cluster-robust and wild cluster bootstrap analyses supported the immediate effect (b = 0.354, cluster-robust SE = 0.065; bootstrap 95% CI [0.140, 0.566]) and the delayed effect (b = 0.225, SE = 0.061; bootstrap 95% CI [0.062, 0.386]). Four weeks later, 59.9% of the immediate gain was retained in the intervention arm and 63.4% of the between-arm effect, estimates consistent with partial retention given their wide intervals. The intervention effect was larger among students who used generative AI more frequently (interaction b = 0.206, cluster-robust p = 0.040). A short, curriculum-embedded information ethics module thus improved university students’ AI ethical judgment, with gains partially retained after four weeks and the largest benefits among frequent users.

item.title: Negotiating epistemic authority in AI-assisted lesson planning: a multiple-case study of preservice mathematics teachers
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can provide preservice teachers with a complete lesson plan before they have articulated the reasoning the plan is intended to develop, creating conditions for automation bias and cognitive offloading. This multiple-case study examined how five preservice mathematics teachers in China negotiated epistemic authority while planning using GenAI. Methods Cases were selected from 42 preservice teachers through preliminary quantitative screening. Screen-recording-derived event logs, concurrent verbalizations, video-stimulated recall interviews, and written reflections were integrated into an evidence matrix comprising 34 decision episodes. Authority was interpreted as retained, shared, or ceded based on the relationship among the source of a proposal, the participant’s action, the warrant invoked, and whether that warrant was enacted in the lesson plan. Results Authority was retained in 16 episodes, shared in 12, and ceded in 6, with variation across cases. Visible actions did not map onto authority positions in a fixed way, and professional warrants were sometimes not enacted. Two vulnerabilities emerged. A closed verification loop, observed in four episodes across two cases, occurred when participants recognized uncertainty about AI output yet asked the same AI to validate it. An insight–action gap, illustrated by three episodes in a single case, occurred when recognized pedagogica problems were not translated into planned teacher responses. Discussion The findings support the proposition that the educative value of AI-assisted planning depends less on how much novices edit AI output than on whether tasks require independent verification and warranted, enacted decisions.

item.title: Mapping digital health intervention components to Bandura’s sources of self-efficacy in cancer care: a scoping review
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Digital health technologies are increasingly used for symptom management, patient education, and continuity of care among people with cancer. However, the relationship between intervention components and theoretical pathways of self-efficacy has not been systematically mapped. Objective This scoping review aimed to describe the types, functional components, implementation characteristics, and self-efficacy outcome directions of digital health technologies designed to support self-efficacy in adults with cancer, and to map these components to Bandura’s sources of self-efficacy information. Methods This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the JBI methodological guidance and reported according to PRISMA-ScR. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, and PsycINFO were searched from inception to January 9, 2026. Studies of digital health interventions for adult patients with cancer that reported self-efficacy outcomes were eligible. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and theory-based coding. Findings were synthesized using descriptive statistics, narrative synthesis, and evidence matrices. Results Twenty-one studies were included. Digital health technologies mainly included mobile applications, online platforms or websites, telehealth-supported care, and wearable devices; some studies integrated artificial intelligence, virtual simulation, text messaging, or other electronic communication tools. Intervention components included health education, self-monitoring, goal setting, task practice, feedback, professional support, peer interaction, reminders, and emotion regulation. Five studies reported significant improvement in overall self-efficacy, three reported improvement in specific dimensions, two reported improvement in high-engagement or subgroup analyses, three showed non-significant positive trends, and eight observed no significant change. In the descriptive comparison, moderate-to-strong mastery-experience coding was observed in all 10 studies reporting statistically significant improvement in overall, domain-specific, or high-engagement/subgroup self-efficacy, compared with 7 of 11 studies not reporting statistically significant improvement. Moderate-to-strong verbal-persuasion coding was observed in 10 of 10 and 6 of 11 studies, respectively. These patterns reflected co-occurrence rather than independent effects. Conclusion Digital health interventions varied substantially in functional components, theoretical operationalization, professional support, engagement, and outcomes. Moderate-to-strong mastery-experience and verbal-persuasion coding was more common among studies reporting statistically significant improvement. Future studies should report intervention components, theoretical pathways, engagement, professional support, and follow-up more consistently.

item.title: From “usefulness” to “dependence”: the dynamic evolution mechanism of generative AI use behaviors
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) rapidly permeates Chinese higher education, university students’ AI use behaviors have come to be characterized by “high frequency, wide penetration, and rapid iteration.” Yet, a systematic understanding of the dynamic evolution mechanism from initial cognition to deep dependence remains lacking. Methods Employing a four-wave longitudinal design spanning 18 months (the first week of June 2024 to the first week of December 2025, with one wave every 6 months) and drawing on 524 valid responses to the 600 distributed questionnaires, retained in full across all four waves, this study systematically investigates the dynamic trajectories and mediating mechanisms of 12 core constructs, including perceived usefulness, trust, technology concerns, ethical concerns, use behavior, technology integration, usage habits, academic dependence, and moral disengagement. Results Repeated-measures ANOVA and mediation model testing reveal the following: (1) Perceived usefulness exhibits an asymmetric U-shaped trajectory of “sharp initial decline, stabilization, and rebound,” which does not support the hypothesized inverted U-shaped pattern. (2) Trust shows a trajectory of “adjusted decline, low-level stabilization, and internalized overshooting,” with an “overshooting” phenomenon in the later stage that surpasses the initial level. (3) Technology concerns decrease in a strictly monotonic fashion, whereas ethical concerns follow an asymmetric U-shaped trajectory of “precipitous decline, stabilization, and sharp rebound,” revealing a differentiated pattern of technological desensitization and ethical re-sensitization. (4) Technology integration partially mediates the transformation from actual use behavior to usage habits (indirect effect proportion = 23.39%), with the cognitive pathway accounting for only about one-quarter of the total association. (5) Early trust significantly and positively predicts continuance intention 18 months later (β = 0.400), and this effect is partially mediated by user satisfaction. (6) Exploratory analyses show that perceived usefulness negatively predicts academic dependence and moral disengagement through the sequential mediation of “actual use behavior → technology integration → usage habits,” suggesting that “high usefulness” may lead to benign autonomous use rather than problematic dependence. Conclusion This study is among the first to adopt a longitudinal design to reveal the nonlinear dynamic evolution patterns of GenAI use behaviors among Chinese university students. It provides crucial empirical evidence for extending technology acceptance theories along the temporal dimension, for understanding the stratified evolution of risk perception, and for informing AI education interventions. The sample was recruited by convenience sampling and consists almost entirely of female students in the humanities and social sciences; the findings describe this sample, and no claim of generalization to all Chinese university students is made.

item.title: From generation to judgment: the multidimensional structure of design thinking mindset and differences across learning stages in AIGC-supported fashion film design learning
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) is changing how design alternatives are generated in fashion film design learning, enabling students to obtain large numbers of comparable and iteratively refinable visual outcomes within a short period. However, expanded generative capacity does not, by itself, determine how learners interpret, evaluate, experiment with, and select among uncertain outcomes. In this human–AI collaborative creative environment, empirical evidence remains limited on whether learners’ design-related psychological tendencies form a distinguishable multidimensional structure that is comparable across learning stages. Design Thinking Mindset (DTM) provides a multidimensional psychological framework for addressing this issue. Methods Drawing on Vignoli et al.’s DTM framework, this study examined five dimensions—Uncertainty and Risk, Empathy, Experimentation, Abductive Reasoning, and Creative Confidence—through a cross-sectional survey of 409 first-year and third-year students from three Chinese universities who had experience with AIGC fashion film design projects. Confirmatory factor analysis and measurement invariance testing across year groups were used to examine the five-dimensional structure and its measurement comparability, followed by latent mean comparisons. Results The five DTM dimensions formed a correlated yet distinguishable structure and demonstrated measurement comparability across year groups. Third-year students had significantly higher latent means on all five dimensions, with the largest descriptive standardized difference point estimates observed for Abductive Reasoning and Creative Confidence. Discussion These findings provide empirical support for the applicability of five selected DTM dimensions in AIGC-supported fashion film design learning and reveal distinct patterns of self-reported psychological tendencies across year groups. From an educational perspective, the results suggest that AIGC-supported design education should attend not only to the generation of creative alternatives but also to learners’ psychological orientations toward uncertainty, experimentation, audience understanding, creative reasoning, and confidence in creative work.

item.title: Generative AI dependency and perceived learning outcomes among university students: an indirect association involving effort regulation
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Objective Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into university learning, raising questions about dependency-oriented reliance and self-regulation. Drawing on a self-regulated learning perspective, this study examined associations among GenAI dependency, effort regulation, and multidimensional perceived learning outcomes, including the statistical indirect association involving effort regulation. Methods Cross-sectional survey data were collected from 982 students at three higher education institutions in Guangdong Province, China. Confirmatory factor analysis and covariance-based structural equation modeling were conducted, with indirect associations tested using 5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples. Sensitivity analyses adjusted for GenAI use frequency. Results The measurement model showed acceptable fit (CFI = 0.953, TLI = 0.944, RMSEA = 0.043, SRMR = 0.041). GenAI dependency showed a small negative total association with perceived learning outcomes ( β = −0.087) and was negatively associated with effort regulation ( β = −0.257). Effort regulation was positively associated with perceived learning outcomes ( β = 0.497). The residual direct association was nonsignificant ( β = 0.041), whereas the indirect association was negative and significant ( β = −0.128). After adjustment for GenAI use frequency, the indirect association remained significant, but the small total association was no longer significant. Conclusion The findings highlight effort regulation as a relevant learner-controlled process in the association between GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes. They also distinguish dependency-oriented reliance from frequency of GenAI use. The cross-sectional design and potential classroom clustering warrant cautious interpretation.

item.title: Perceived AI literacy and TPACK in pre-service teacher education: mediating roles of perceived usefulness, ease of use, and value in blended learning
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into blended learning requires pre-service teachers to develop AI-related competencies and the ability to integrate technology into pedagogy. This study examines how perceived AI literacy and technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK) are associated with deep learning through perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and perceived value of AI use. Methods A cross-sectional survey was completed by 423 pre-service teachers enrolled in blended learning courses at a university in China. Data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), with covariance-based structural equation modeling and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) used as complementary robustness and configurational analyses. Results Perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and perceived value of AI use significantly mediated the relationships between the two competencies and deep learning. All six indirect pathways were significant in both the PLS-SEM and covariance-based SEM analyses. The fsQCA revealed an equifinal and asymmetric structure: multiple, partly substitutable conditions were sufficient for high deep learning, and no single condition was necessary for either high or low deep learning. Conclusions The findings integrate the technology acceptance model and expectancy-value theory to explain how pre-service teachers' competencies and perceptions relate to deep learning in AI-enhanced blended environments. Teacher education should support technical competence alongside positive perceptions of AI's utility, usability, and value. Because the measures were self-reported and collected cross-sectionally at one university, the findings are interpreted as associational and configurational rather than causal.

item.title: Teachers’ basic psychological need satisfactions and their intentions to use generative artificial intelligence: the mediating role of engagement in professional development
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers new opportunities for instructional innovation, yet the psychological mechanisms underlying teachers’ intentions to adopt it remain unclear. Intrinsic motivation is an important internal factor shaping teachers’ intentions to use GenAI and is closely linked to the satisfaction of their basic psychological needs. Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT), this study develops and tests a theoretical framework linking teachers’ basic psychological need satisfaction to their intention to use GenAI through intrinsic motivation and engagement in professional development. Such engagement may foster innovation in GenAI-supported teaching practices. Methods Survey data were collected from 146 teachers participating in a GenAI learning program. Structural equation modeling was used to examine the hypothesized relationships among basic psychological need satisfaction, intrinsic motivation, engagement in professional development, and intention to use GenAI. Results Perceived competence in using GenAI was significantly and positively associated with intrinsic motivation, whereas perceived autonomy and relatedness were not significantly associated with intrinsic motivation. Engagement in professional development mediated the relationship between intrinsic motivation and intention to use GenAI. Discussion These findings provide a nuanced understanding of the psychological mechanisms underlying teachers’ intentions to adopt GenAI, highlighting the roles of perceived competence, intrinsic motivation, and engagement in professional development. They also offer practical implications for supporting the integration of GenAI into teaching.

item.title: Teachers’ attitudes and behavioural intentions towards AI integration in Chinese higher education: a qualitative interview study
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction The rapid expansion of generative AI has intensified scholarly and policy debate over its role in higher education, yet university teachers’ attitudes towards its integration remain complex and context-dependent. This study explores how university teachers perceive, experience, and respond to AI integration in their teaching. Guided primarily by the three-component attitude model and informed by the technology acceptance model and the theory of planned behaviour, the study examines cognitive appraisals, affective responses, behavioural intentions, and perceived support needs. Methods The study draws on semi-structured interviews with 14 university teachers from four higher education institutions in China. The interview data were analysed using codebook-informed thematic analysis combining deductive and inductive coding. Results The findings indicate that teachers generally perceive AI as a supportive rather than substitutive educational tool, valuing it for improving efficiency, supporting lesson preparation, and enriching pedagogical design. Emotional responses varied from enthusiasm and a sense of accomplishment to caution, neutrality, and, in some cases, declining satisfaction. Across the interviews, teachers’ primary concerns centred less on their own replacement than on the perceived risks of inappropriate AI use for students’ independent thinking, reasoning, originality, and authentic understanding. Teachers’ intentions to adopt AI were therefore conditional and bounded, shaped by pedagogical purpose, disciplinary context, student readiness, and the need to maintain teacher control. Teachers also emphasised that sustainable AI integration requires more than general encouragement, calling instead for AI literacy development, discipline-sensitive support, specialised tools, and enabling institutional infrastructure. Discussion Overall, these findings extend contextual understandings of teachers’ AI acceptance by showing how adoption intentions are pedagogically negotiated and highlight the importance of supporting professional judgement and students’ independent thinking in higher education.

item.title: Human-in-the-loop semantic learning analytics for assessing moral-value reasoning in university AI ethics education
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction University AI ethics education addresses fairness, privacy, accountability, transparency, human autonomy, and academic integrity, but the semantic structure of students' moral-value reasoning and its connection to responsible solutions remain insufficiently characterized. This study examined a human-in-the-loop semantic learning analytics framework for task-specific moral-value reasoning. Methods Ninety science and engineering graduate students completed an online explicit-reflective AI ethics module in a one-group pre–post multimethod study without a control group. Assessments comprised an AI ethics knowledge test, a perceived-awareness scale, and open-ended ethical reasoning tasks. Expert annotations informed transformer-based multi-label coding, descriptive value coverage and balance metrics, problem–solution coupling, and baseline-only nested cross-validated prediction of subsequent raw problem-solving change. Results Within-participant pre–post increases were observed in ethical knowledge, perceived moral-value awareness, actual ethical awareness, problem–solving skills, value coverage, value balance, and problem–solution coupling. Automated semantic coding achieved participant-grouped cross-validated macro-F1 = 0.83 (95% CI [0.78, 0.87]; micro-F1 = 0.86; macro-AUPRC = 0.82). The baseline-only prediction model yielded cross-validated R 2 = 0.30 (95% CI [0.11, 0.45]) for subsequent raw problem-solving change. Discussion Expert-supervised semantic analytics can characterize value representation and issue–solution reasoning in AI ethics assessments. Coverage and balance describe response structure rather than moral quality. The absence of a control group, repeated use of one scenario, and modest sample size preclude causal and broad trait-level conclusions.

item.title: Uneven automation: comparing authorship anxiety and generative AI use among art and design undergraduate students
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Art and design education expects students to develop a sense of authorship over original work, but generative AI (GenAI) complicates how students understand and claim that authorship. This study examined whether these experiences differ across creative fields through a mixed-methods design. The survey included 2,441 GenAI-using students from seven field categories at 33 art and design institutions in China and assessed authorship anxiety, creative agency, perceived usefulness, dependence on GenAI, and frequency of use. The quantitative analysis first examined variation across all seven categories and then compared fine art with the five applied design fields. Interview data from 22 survey participants were also examined thematically. The main findings include that (1) authorship anxiety did not differ significantly across the seven categories or between fine art and pooled design; the latter comparison met the equivalence criterion at ±d = 0.20, but not at tighter bounds; (2) clearer differences emerged in how students used GenAI. Compared with fine-art students, design students considered GenAI more useful and used it more frequently; (3) across the interviews, most students described authorship as retaining control over the creative idea while delegating parts of its execution to GenAI. Specifically, fine-art students often grounded authorship in embodied making and human imperfection, whereas design students placed greater emphasis on judgement, selection, and control. We call this pattern uneven automation: concern about authorship was broadly shared, but students in different fields responded to GenAI in different ways, potentially reflecting the varying labour-market pressures surrounding their disciplines.

item.title: Low-dimensional burnout risk classification in engineering students: the role of demand-recovery interaction features
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Student burnout is a rapidly growing concern, with prior research linking its development to a wide range of psychological, behavioral, and contextual factors. Machine learning approaches have recently shown strong predictive performance for identifying burnout, but typically rely on high-dimensional datasets impractical for real-world use. Whether burnout can be reliably identified from a minimal set of variables remains underexplored. This study addresses that gap using a low-dimensional predictive framework in undergraduate engineering students. Grounded in Conservation of Resources theory, three classifiers (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) were evaluated across three feature configurations (Raw: all nine unengineered base predictors, including academic, demographic, sleep, and physical activity variables; Engineered: four demand–recovery interaction features; Full: Raw combined with Engineered) to test whether burnout reflects academic load alone or an imbalance between demand and recovery capacity. The Full configuration performed best: Logistic Regression and Random Forest exceeded a matched permutation-based null (Global MCC = 0.173 and 0.190, respectively, p < 0.05), while Gradient Boosting did not reach significance (MCC = 0.126, p = 0.066). Across 50 alternative fold splits, however, mean Global MCC for the Full configuration was lower for each classifier (Logistic Regression 0.09, Random Forest 0.16, Gradient Boosting 0.11), indicating that the primary-split estimates are upper-range. In addition, adding engineered features to Raw predictors did not produce a statistically distinguishable improvement in Global MCC for any classifier. Moderate Risk classification remained difficult across all classifiers and configurations, with most confidence intervals crossing zero. Permutation importance identified Workload-Sleep Strain as the most influential predictor in the Random Forest model, suggesting the engineered features capture meaningful behavioral patterns. However, because these variables are deterministic transformations of the raw predictors, their incremental contribution could not be confirmed statistically. These results offer preliminary evidence that a small set of sleep, activity, workload, and engineered variables carries predictive signal for burnout risk above chance.

item.title: Should there be a teacher in-the-loop? A study of generative AI-personalized tasks middle school
item.description:
Educational Technology Research and Development
Abstract Large language models can be used to design instructional tasks to align to students’ needs. These generative AI models can create tasks that correspond to students’ out-of-school interests in areas like sports or music, which may enhance students’ interest in learning. However, little is known about teachers’ processes for creating or modifying tasks with generative AI, despite commercial AI companies’ claims that they will save teachers time. In the present study, 7 middle school mathematics teachers used ChatGPT to create personalized versions of problems in their curriculum to correspond to their students’ interests. The prompting moves teachers made and their students’ open-ended feedback on personalized problems were examined through thematic analysis. Teachers’ efficiency when creating problems and the ratings of their 7th grade students who received personalized assignments were examined. Results from this sample suggest that having a teacher-in-the-loop may result in generative AI-enhanced personalization being enacted at a broad grain size, whereas students often expressed preference for a smaller grain-size where they receive specific popular culture references that interest them. Teachers used prompting to adjust popular culture references and address issues with the depth, ethics, or realism of the problems generated, in some cases showing epistemic agency. The article closes with an exploratory, design-focused look at scalability trade-offs with teacher-facing personalization, patterns of teacher prompting practices, and opportunities for teachers to exercise epistemic and ethical monitoring of personalization outputs.

item.title: Exploring student and teacher perspectives on critical thinking with generative AI: early insights from the EduPartnerAI platform
item.description:
Smart Learning Environments
Abstract The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education has raised important questions about its implications for students’ analytical reasoning and independent judgment. ChatGPT, a generative AI model capable of producing human-like responses, is widely used in academic contexts, yet its educational value requires careful evaluation. This paper presents and evaluates EduPartnerAI, a platform that integrates ChatGPT into student assignments and is designed to encourage critical engagement with AI-generated content. The platform records student-AI interactions, requires students to reflect on ChatGPT’s outputs, and provides teachers with tools to review observable indicators of student reasoning and AI response quality. An exploratory study involving 61 undergraduate students was conducted, relying on student reflection questionnaires, a usability survey, teacher evaluations, and an analysis of recorded interactions. Students generally perceived ChatGPT as a useful learning tool that provided clear explanations and practical examples, although some recognized that its responses could be overly general or incomplete. The teacher observed that students asked relevant questions and effectively incorporated AI-generated content into their assignments but experienced some difficulties with error detection, independent judgment, and critical evaluation. The teacher also judged ChatGPT’s outputs to be largely relevant, clear, and accurate, with few instances of bias or misleading information. Overall, the findings provide preliminary insights into student and teacher perspectives and observable patterns of engagement, highlighting both the educational potential of generative AI and the need for appropriate instructional scaffolding.

item.title: Editrail: Understanding AI Usage by Visualizing Student-AI Interaction in Code
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Programming instructors have diverse philosophies about integrating generative AI into their classes. Some encourage students to use AI, while others restrict or forbid it. Regardless of their approach, all instructors benefit from understanding how their students actually use AI while writing code [1, 14, 25, 38]. Such insight helps instructors assess whether AI use aligns with their pedagogical goals, enables timely intervention when they find unproductive usage patterns, and establishes effective policies for AI use. However, our survey with programming instructors found that many instructors lack visibility into how students use AI in their code-writing processes. To address this challenge, we introduce Editrail, an interactive system that enables instructors to track students’ AI usage, create personalized assessments, and provide timely interventions, all within the workflow of monitoring coding histories. We found that Editrail enables instructors to accurately detect AI use that conflicts with pedagogical goals and to determine when and which students require intervention.

item.title: TeachUp: Facilitating Early-Stage Teachers to Learn Instructional Strategies from Classroom Videos with Reflective Support
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Recorded videos of offline open classes provide good examples for early-stage teachers to learn instructional strategies, e.g., how to organize cooperative learning. However, learning by watching these videos is challenging, as these strategies are implicitly performed, and it lacks in-situ reflective support. In this paper, via a formative study (N=9), we design TeachUp to support the learning of instructional strategies from classroom teaching videos. TeachUp adopts an LLM-powered pipeline to detect nine instructional strategies in videos (precision = 63.4%), provides reflective questions and hints while watching, and generates customized practices with reflective feedback. A within-subjects study (N=16) shows that compared to a traditional video-playing and self-practicing baseline, early-stage teachers with TeachUp are more engaged in learning and perform better in applying learned strategies to new tasks. Interviews with four in-service teachers further generalize our findings and TeachUp’s use cases. We discuss practical implications for fostering video-based learning of instructional strategies.

item.title: Democratizing Extensive Reading by Tailoring Web Content
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Extensive reading helps foreign language learners build proficiency through large amounts of interesting, level-appropriate text. However, providing enough material matched to learners’ interests and evolving proficiency is resource-intensive and difficult to sustain. To address this challenge, we present Adapt-ER, a browser extension that leverages the web to support scalable self-selected reading by adapting pages in place to each learner’s vocabulary profile. Adapt-ER estimates lexical proficiency, tailors web content in real time, and supports lightweight profile refinement through click-based interactive learner feedback during reading. To make adaptation practical during live browsing, we compare LLM-based strategies and develop a hybrid pipeline that balances lexical difficulty control, semantic preservation, latency, and cost. In a within-subject study, Adapt-ER increased reading speed, reduced the need for dictionary and translation support during reading, and improved self-reported engagement. Our findings suggest that in-place adaptation of self-selected web text can make web reading better suited to sustained extensive reading.

item.title: PACEE: Parent-Centered AI Scaffolding for Emotion Education in Early Childhood Conversations
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Emotion education is critical for children aged 3 to 6. However, existing technologies depend substantially on direct child-AI interaction, overlooking the central role of parents in guiding early emotional development at home. To address this gap, we conducted co-design sessions with five kindergarten teachers and five parents to identify key parental challenges and opportunities for AI support in family emotion education. Based on these insights, we developed PACEE, an LLM-based assistant designed around an asymmetric triadic interaction framework: AI primarily supports parents while preserving parent-child interaction. PACEE provides parent-centered AI scaffolding that supports parents in real-time conversation through personalized guidance, post-hoc reflection through trackable feedback, and understanding children’s emotional states through modeling. We evaluated PACEE with 16 families. Results showed that PACEE increased parent-child conversational engagement and improved parents’ overall experience when guiding emotion-related conversations. Together, we contribute an asymmetric triadic interaction framework for AI-supported family education, offering design insights for AI systems that support parents while preserving parent-led parent–child interaction.

item.title: Explorable Proofs: Making Written Proofs Explorable by Grounding Them in Formal Representations
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
LLM-generated explanations can make technical content more accessible, but there is a ceiling on what they can support interactively. Because LLM outputs are static text, they cannot be executed, tinkered with, or stepped through. In this paper, we explore how grounding explanations in a formalized representation enables interactive affordances beyond what static text supports. We instantiate this idea for mathematical proof comprehension in explorable proofs, an approach that uses LLMs to translate a theorem and its written proof into Lean, a programming language for machine-checked proofs, and links the written proof with the Lean code. Readers can work through the proof at a step-level granularity, test custom examples or counterexamples, and trace the logical dependencies bridging between steps. Each worked-out step is produced by executing the Lean proof on an example and extracting its intermediate state. A user study (n = 16) shows potential advantages of this approach: in a proof-understanding task, participants who used the explorability features wrote proof descriptions that an instructor preferred over those written with a proof-and-chatbot baseline, and gave more correct and more detailed answers to proof comprehension questions.

item.title: Interactively Teaching Collaborative Physical Tasks to Generative AI with Narrated Demonstrations
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Enabling users to teach computers how to perform physical tasks is a long-standing goal in HCI. Prior work has explored learning from demonstration, but demonstrations often underspecify intent. Advances in generative AI enable a combination of demonstration and verbal narration to disambiguate intent. However, it remains largely unexplored how to design interfaces that leverage such narrated demonstrations to teach collaborative physical tasks. To probe this design space, we present a prototype system, Apprento, that models physical tasks as programs via generative AI with three integrated interfaces: (1) a teaching interface for providing narrated demonstrations in mixed reality, (2) an inspection interface for visualizing generated programs as decision-flow diagrams and program executions, and (3) a correction interface for iteratively refining generated programs. Across these interfaces, narrated demonstrations serve as a communication modality between users and the system. In a study with 20 participants teaching soccer skills, we identify differing user expectations around authoring and teaching collaborative tasks, as well as key design tensions between task complexity and program interpretability, and between program expressivity and accuracy. We discuss implications for designing future systems that support symbolic modeling of collaborative physical tasks through narrated demonstrations.

item.title: Who's Keeping Score? Interactive Steering of LLM-Powered Scoring with Attune
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to score text records at scale (e.g., rating candidate resumes on a 1–5 scale). However, existing LLM-powered approaches do not account for the fact that effective scoring requires both holistic understanding of records and locally consistent judgments across similar ones. We present Attune, a mixed-initiative system for steerable LLM-powered scoring. Given a task description and scoring range, Attune performs pairwise comparisons across records to develop a global understanding first, and then resolves these comparisons into consistent score assignments—deriving scoring criteria and rules bottom-up in the process. These serve as shared representations of scoring logic that users can inspect and edit. Based on insights from a formative study (n = 12), Attune’s interface introduces novel steering interactions that allow users to deterministically refine scoring logic. Users can provide examples, directly edit criteria, rules, or target distributions, and give natural language feedback—with all refinements compiling into constraints that guide re-scoring. We validate our approach through a technical evaluation across three workloads and a user study with domain experts (n = 8) in healthcare, law, education, and AI evaluation.

item.title: MAIC-UI: Making Interactive Courseware with Generative UI
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Creating interactive STEM courseware traditionally requires HTML/CSS/JavaScript expertise, leaving barriers for educators. While generative AI can produce HTML codes, existing tools generate static presentations rather than interactive simulations, struggle with long documents, and lack pedagogical accuracy mechanisms. Furthermore, full regeneration for modifications requires 200–600 seconds, disrupting creative flow. We present MAIC-UI, a zero-code authoring system that enables educators to create and rapidly edit interactive courseware from textbooks, PPTs, and PDFs. MAIC-UI employs: (1) structured knowledge analysis with multi-modal understanding to ensure pedagogical rigor; (2) a two-stage generate-verify-optimize pipeline separating content alignment from visual refinement; and (3) Click-to-Locate editing with Unified Diff-based incremental generation achieving sub-10-second iteration cycles. A controlled lab study with 40 participants shows MAIC-UI reduces editing iterations (4.9 vs. 7.0) and significantly improves learnability and controllability compared to direct Text-to-HTML generation. A three-month classroom deployment with 53 high school students demonstrates that MAIC-UI fosters learning agency and reduces outcome disparities—the pilot class achieved 9.21-point gains in STEM subjects compared to -2.32 points in control classes. Our code is available at https://github.com/THU-MAIC/MAIC-UI.

item.title: CinemaWorld: Generative Augmented Reality with LLMs and 3D Scene Generation for Movie Augmentation
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
We introduce CinemaWorld, a generative augmented reality system that augments the viewer’s physical surroundings with automatically generated mixed reality 3D content extracted from and synchronized with 2D movie scenes. Our system preprocesses films to extract key features using multimodal large language models (LLMs), generates dynamic 3D augmentations with generative AI, and embeds them spatially into the viewer’s physical environment on the Meta Quest 3. To identify key augmentation techniques for CinemaWorld, we conducted an elicitation study with eight film students, which led us to identify several key augmentation types, including particle effects, surrounding objects, textural overlays, character-driven augmentation, and lighting effects. We evaluated our system through a technical evaluation (N=100 video clips), a user evaluation (comparison study: N=12 and in-the-wild study: N=8), and expert interviews with film creators (N=8). Results indicate that CinemaWorld enhances immersion and enjoyment, suggesting its potential to enrich the film-viewing experience.

item.title: TailorCoPilot: Enabling Agentic Pattern Making with Version-Controlled State Tracking
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Experience-driven manufacturing, such as garment pattern making, faces a severe generational skills gap because its core expertise relies on undocumented tacit knowledge forged through day-to-day practice. To address this challenge, we present TailorCoPilot, an agentic pattern-making system built upon a specially designed version-control backend TailorTrace. TailorTrace models sewing patterns as structured, discrete states and records their transformations during the pattern-making process as explicit operation sequences defined upon the geometry primitives in the sewing pattern (panels, edges, vertices and stitches). Integrated into a conventional pattern-making GUI, TailorTrace enables seamless documentation of senior experts’ tacit pattern-making knowledge without breaking their daily workflow. The documented knowledge further offers interactive, pedagogical scaffolding for novices, while providing a robust foundation to power TailorCoPilot and train future generative AI models. In a user study with novices and advanced novices, TailorCoPilot improved task completion rates, reduced time and perceived workload, and yielded higher-quality artifacts compared to skill-appropriate baselines. Ultimately, TailorCoPilot demonstrates a viable pathway to capture practice-based expertise, operationalizing it to support both generative AI advancements and human apprenticeship.

item.title: PATHWiSE: Empowering Teachers with a Generative AI Authoring System for Personalized Robot-Assisted Learning
item.description:
ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
Homework assignments often lack the personalized guidance and social interaction crucial for learning. Social robots offer a promising way to bring personalization and interactive support into learning activities; however, teachers rarely have the technical expertise needed to operate robots, let alone create or customize robot-assisted learning (RAL) lessons. To address this challenge, we introduce PATHWiSE, a robust, no-code authoring system designed to empower teachers to create custom RAL activities. Developed through participatory co-design activities with middle school science teachers and students and iteratively refined through multiple user studies, PATHWiSE enables educators to author, preview, and personalize RAL activities that can be tailored to different robot platforms and delivered with either in-person or on-screen robots. The system maintains a flexible trigger-action programming model to define robot expressions contextually related to lesson materials. Through integrated teacher- and student-facing portals, teachers can deploy RAL lessons using a lightweight and portable browser-based approach that affords integration with a wide range of systems. AI-assisted comment and emotion-expression generation tools augment teacher lesson creation while preserving teacher autonomy and expertise in content design. In this paper, we present the design and implementation of PATHWiSE, including its authoring workflow, interface architecture, backend integration, and representative use cases drawn from iterative studies to illustrate the capabilities of the full system.

item.title: As effective as the teacher, but less motivating: a randomized controlled comparison of AI-generated and teacher feedback on students’ writing performance and intrinsic motivation
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers scalable feedback on student writing; however, its effects on writing performance and motivation relative to teacher feedback remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on Feedback Intervention Theory and Self-Determination Theory, this study examined the comparative effectiveness of AI-generated and teacher-provided feedback on students’ writing performance and motivational outcomes. Methods A randomized controlled study assigned 312 undergraduate students to one of three conditions: AI-generated feedback, teacher feedback, or a control condition without substantive feedback. A total of 287 participants were included in the analyses. The study evaluated revised-essay quality, feedback engagement, writing self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, perceived relatedness to the feedback source, and AI literacy. Results Both AI-generated feedback and teacher feedback produced higher revised-essay quality than the control condition, with effect sizes of d = 0.60 and d = 0.59, respectively. The two feedback conditions were statistically equivalent within a prespecified equivalence margin of ±0.35 standard deviations. Feedback engagement, but not writing self-efficacy, statistically accounted for the observed performance advantage. Teacher feedback elicited higher intrinsic motivation than AI-generated feedback, although AI-generated feedback also yielded higher intrinsic motivation than the control condition. This motivational difference was associated with perceived relatedness to the feedback source. The indirect effects identified in the analyses are associational rather than causal. AI literacy did not significantly moderate the effect of feedback on writing performance ( p = 0.058). Discussion Within the context of a single feedback-and-revision cycle at one institution, the findings suggest that AI-generated feedback can achieve writing-performance outcomes comparable to those of teacher feedback, while providing weaker motivational support. These results highlight the potential value of blended feedback approaches that combine the scalability of AI-generated feedback with the relational and motivational strengths of teacher–student interaction. Further research across multiple institutions and repeated feedback cycles is needed to establish the generalizability and longer-term implications of these findings.

item.title: Making argumentative work visible in GenAI-mediated assessment: an exploratory LLM simulation and questionnaire study in university ideological and political education
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative AI weakens the correspondence between the final text of an assignment and the argumentative work involved in producing it. This study examined how task structure and AI-use instructions shape evidence use, engagement with objections, and revision in university ideological and political education. Methods An LLM simulation crossed three task formats—position essays, evidence-integration memoranda, and follow-up-and-revision defense tasks—with three AI-use scenarios—simulated no-AI, responsible collaboration, and concealed ghostwriting. Two raters coded 148 generated texts with the Textual Response Artifact Scoring Index (TRASI), and an anonymous questionnaire collected 268 evaluations of 27 selected texts. Results Responsible collaboration produced the highest overall rubric score ( M = 3.32). Evidence-integration memoranda ( M = 3.16) and follow-up-and-revision defenses ( M = 3.10) exceeded position essays ( M = 2.63). Position essays varied most across the three AI-use scenarios, whereas the memorandum and defense showed narrower differences because their instructions already required source explanation or response and revision. Questionnaire participants distinguished the same task functions: memoranda were rated highest for source–claim linkage, and defenses for counterargument response and revision explanation. Open-ended responses associated evidence integration, comparison of reasons, and revision with thinking, while formulaic structure, over-polished expression, and generic abstraction were associated with AI-like writing. Discussion Task structure and AI-use instructions were functionally complementary. Structured tasks elicited source explanation or challenge and revision directly, so responsible collaboration added its largest contribution in the general position essay. GenAI-mediated assessment can therefore be designed around the argumentative decisions that writers are required to document.

item.title: From Narrative to Intent Schema Architecture: An Artificial Intelligence System for Human-Centered Advising Decision Support
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Transfer advising is a high-uncertainty setting where students rarely ask well-structured questions and advisors must infer intent from fragmented narratives across conflicting institutional policies. This research presents a human-centered AI framework that transforms naturalistic student discourse into structured advising intents, supporting a student-facing advising assistant whose explainable outputs are designed to support advisor review. Using 19,668 transfer-related Reddit posts, it surfaces recurring advising intents via extraction, clustering, and structured labeling, then routes student questions to them. On a proof-of-concept benchmark it reached 90% intent-level and 86% question-level accuracy, turning advising knowledge into transparent structures that support scalable, human-centered advising.

item.title: Autonomy satisfaction and bedtime procrastination among generation Z university students: The serial mediating roles of general self-efficacy and AI dependence
item.description:
Acta Psychologica
BACKGROUND: With the rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education, university students' daily behaviors are increasingly shaped by technology use. Bedtime procrastination has emerged as a common self-regulation problem among Generation Z students. However, the psychological mechanisms linking environmental resources and technology-related behaviors to sleep outcomes remain insufficiently understood. This study examined the associations between autonomy satisfaction and bedtime procrastination and the mediating roles of general self-efficacy and AI dependence. METHODS: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 717 Chinese university students using cluster sampling. Standardized self-report measures assessed autonomy satisfaction, general self-efficacy, AI dependence, and bedtime procrastination. Data were analyzed using SPSS 26.0 and Mplus 8.0. Structural equation modeling and bias-corrected bootstrap (5000 resamples) were employed to test direct and indirect effects. RESULTS: Autonomy satisfaction was positively associated with general self-efficacy and negatively associated with AI dependence and bedtime procrastination. General self-efficacy was negatively associated with both AI dependence and bedtime procrastination, while AI dependence was positively associated with bedtime procrastination. Mediation analysis revealed that both general self-efficacy and AI dependence served as significant mediators, with AI dependence accounting for a larger proportion of the indirect effect. A significant serial mediation pathway was also observed. CONCLUSIONS: The findings suggest that autonomy satisfaction was associated with bedtime procrastination through both cognitive and behavioral mechanisms. AI dependence plays a particularly important role as a proximal behavioral pathway. These results highlight the need to promote balanced AI use and strengthen students' self-regulation in technology-rich learning environments.

item.title: ChatGPT ‐Supported Literary Translation: Tense Accuracy and Dynamic Emotion Profiles in the Language Classroom
item.description:
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning
ABSTRACT Background Generative artificial intelligence can facilitate task completion, but whether it improves learning or consistently shapes task‐related emotions remains unclear. Objectives This mixed‐methods classroom study compared literary translation with ChatGPT access, translation with dictionary access and optional teacher assistance and regular instruction, focusing on tense accuracy and task‐related emotional experiences. Methods The study involved 42 English‐major undergraduates. All participants completed a pretest and a posttest of English tense use. The 29 students in the translation conditions completed six translation tasks and provided 556 repeated emotion‐bar records with concurrent written explanations; 10 of these students also participated in interviews. Robust analysis of covariance, within‐participant models, exploratory configurational measures and thematic analysis were used. Results Mean scores increased in all three conditions, but adjusted posttest scores and gain scores did not differ significantly among them. No statistically significant between‐condition differences were detected in individual‐emotion percentages or configurational measures. None of the six emotion percentages varied significantly across task sessions, although curiosity was lower at the fourth than at the first measurement point. Profile mixedness was lower in Task 5 (Session 6) than in Task 2 (Session 3). Qualitative findings linked emotions mainly to text content and difficulty, progress, time pressure and classroom conditions. ChatGPT was valued for its speed and immediacy but raised concerns about reliability, effort and ownership. Conclusion The study did not detect a statistically significant advantage for ChatGPT support in tense accuracy or emotional experience. The exploratory configurational analysis nevertheless identified a task‐session difference not apparent in the separate emotion percentages, illustrating the value of examining learning outcomes, repeated emotion reports and students' appraisals together when evaluating AI‐supported language tasks.

item.title: Beyond Access: How GenAI Literacy Relates to Task Performance, Motivation, Cognitive Load and Interaction Patterns in AI ‐Assisted Learning Environment
item.description:
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning
ABSTRACT Background Generative AI is rapidly being integrated into educational settings, yet equitable benefits depend heavily on students' GenAI literacy. While access to these tools is increasing, empirical evidence remains limited on how specific dimensions of assessed GenAI literacy relate to students' task performance, cognitive experiences, and actual interactional behaviours during learning. Objectives This study examined the associations of overall GenAI literacy and its four dimensions (Know and Understand, Use and Apply, Evaluate and Create, Ethics) with students' abstract‐writing performance, self‐efficacy, motivation, and cognitive load. It also explored how assessed literacy is reflected in the configurations of students' interactions with GenAI. Methods A total of 162 university students completed an abstract‐writing task using a custom GenAI assistant. Ordinary least‐squares regression models evaluated the continuous GenAI literacy scores against writing performance, motivation, and cognitive load, adjusting for prior academic writing knowledge and English proficiency. Additionally, Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) was applied to conversational trace data to compare the configurations of questioning and commanding behaviours between higher‐ and lower‐literacy students. Results and Conclusions Higher overall GenAI literacy was positively associated with better writing performance and negatively associated with perceived mental load. Dimension‐level analyses revealed distinct roles: the Use and Apply dimension was independently associated with higher writing performance, while the Know and Understand dimension was uniquely associated with lower mental load. Neither the total score nor the sub‐dimensions showed reliable associations with motivation or self‐efficacy. Furthermore, ENA profiles demonstrated that higher‐literacy students engaged in a refinement‐oriented process, whereas lower‐literacy students relied predominantly on direct content generation and factual retrieval. These findings suggest that instruction should address both conceptual understanding and practical application of GenAI, helping students critically evaluate and refine AI‐generated content during writing.

item.title: Supporting creative agency: metacognitive control and trust in generative AI art education
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
This paper employs a quantitative multimethod design to extend the UTAUT framework for generative AI (GenAI) adoption among art students. Study 1 tested the integrated model via structural equation modeling using cross-sectional survey data from 450 Chinese art students and developed a trust construct grounded in instrumental technology trust, supplemented by art-value-aligned items. Trust in GenAI showed the strongest direct association with behavioral intention ( β = 0.425). Social influence was the dominant correlate of trust ( β = 0.262), with 42.1% of its total effect mediated indirectly through trust. Metacognitive control showed a positive direct association with behavioral intention ( β = 0.146), alongside an indirect association through trust. The structural model based on survey data explained 59.7% of the variance in behavioral intention. Study 2 used a between-subjects experiment with 80 art students to test whether situational metacognitive prompting causally affected creative output. Participants receiving metacognitive prompts (Group A) obtained higher expert ratings than the control group (Group B) on semantic content ( d = 0.67), visual style ( d = 1.30), and spatial composition ( d = 0.63); within-group feature-distance analyses also indicated greater output diversity in Group A across all three dimensions. These findings suggest that trust and metacognitive control are key pathways in GenAI adoption for artistic creation, and that low-cost situational metacognitive prompting may enhance both the quality and diversity of AI-assisted artworks.

item.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education and graduate employability: cognitive engagement, self-efficacy, and career adaptability in the AI era
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is increasingly used in higher education, but its contribution to graduate employability cannot be inferred from access to AI or frequency of use alone. This critical narrative review examines how AI-supported learning may relate to employability through processes discussed in educational psychology and career development. Searches of Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC, and PubMed covered database inception to 1 July 2026, with supplementary searches completed on 2 October 2026. The literature was synthesized interpretively and critically, with attention to the type of outcome measured and the extent to which findings support the proposed relationships. The synthesis focuses on cognitive engagement and self-regulated learning, self-efficacy and motivational regulation, and career adaptability. Three tensions organize the discussion: capability augmentation and cognitive offloading, career agency and AI-related insecurity, and resource access and capability differences. Included studies report associations or short-term changes in outcomes such as engagement, AI literacy, self-efficacy, career adaptability, and perceived employability. Direct evidence linking AI-supported learning to later employment outcomes remains limited. The proposed framework should therefore be read as a set of theory-informed pathways for future testing, rather than as an established causal or temporal sequence. Implications for assessment, disciplinary AI literacy, career education, institutional support, and future research are discussed.

item.title: Symmetrical and asymmetrical insights into student adoption of AI-enhanced digital educational systems
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Based on the stimulus–organism–response (SOR) model and the technology acceptance model (TAM), this study investigates how the functional and experiential features of artificial intelligence (AI)-enhanced educational systems influence users’ behavioral intention through perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use. Methods A multi-method approach integrating partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM), artificial neural networks (ANN) and necessary condition analysis (NCA) was employed. Results The results of the PLS-SEM analysis indicate that both perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use have a significant positive impact on behavioral intention, with perceived ease of use exerting the strongest effect. Furthermore, the effects of functional and experiential features on perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use are asymmetric. ANN analysis confirms the robustness of the findings and identifies perceived ease of use as the most influential determinant of behavioral intention. In contrast, the NCA analysis indicates that perceived usefulness is the only statistically significant necessary condition for achieving higher levels of behavioral intention. Although this necessary relationship is statistically significant, its effect size is small, suggesting that its actual constraining effect is relatively limited. The bottleneck analysis further reveals the constraining characteristics of different stages in the formation of behavioral intention. Discussion By integrating symmetric, asymmetric and necessity-based analytical perspectives, this study provides a more comprehensive understanding of user acceptance behavior in AI-enhanced educational environments.

item.title: Critical AI literacy as a buffer against AI overtrust in students
item.description:
BMC Psychology
Abstract Background The growing use of AI tools such as ChatGPT in academic settings has raised concerns about AI overtrust, yet its psychological correlates remain poorly understood. This study examined how academic self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, and extrinsic motivation are associated with AI overtrust, and tested the sequential mediating roles of performance expectancy and AI literacy in these relationships. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 300 university students in South Korea who had prior experience using AI tools for academic purposes. The questionnaire measured academic self-efficacy, intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, AI literacy, and AI overtrust. Serial mediation analysis was conducted using the PROCESS macro [1] to test direct and indirect effects, including pathways sequentially mediated by performance expectancy and AI literacy. Indirect effects were evaluated using 5,000 bootstrap samples with bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals. Results Academic self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation were both positively associated with AI overtrust: learners who reported higher confidence and greater autonomy also reported higher overtrust in AI-generated information. Extrinsic motivation was numerically more strongly associated with AI overtrust than intrinsic motivation. AI literacy was not significantly correlated with AI overtrust at the bivariate level, but showed a significant negative indirect association within the mediation model. Sequential mediation analysis further indicated that, across all three psychological traits, higher performance expectancy combined with higher AI literacy was associated with lower AI overtrust. Conclusions These findings suggest that learners with higher academic self-efficacy and stronger intrinsic motivation also tend to report higher AI overtrust. Although greater academic self-efficacy may reflect more autonomous use of AI tools, it was nonetheless associated with higher overtrust in the present sample. AI literacy education tailored to learners’ psychological profiles may help support critical thinking, ethical awareness, and responsible AI use.

item.title: Team Cognition in Adversarial Cyber Operations: Effects of Collaboration on Deception Susceptibility and Exploit Behavior
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Cyber-attacks are increasingly carried out by cooperative groups, while current models of cyber deception studies assume an individual actor who is making decisions independently of others. The present study explores the effect of collaboration on exploit behavior and susceptibility to deception in a highly deceptive cyber environment. Specifically, using the Team HackIT human-in-the-loop simulation system, 40 undergraduate computer science students were asked to perform cyber exploitation tasks within a ring topology network in which 75% of the computers were honeypots. The participants worked either in isolation or in collaboration with their partners through a real-time communication tool. It was found that working together substantially increased exploit behavior and honeypot interaction, although it did not help the participants differentiate between legitimate machines and deceptive assets. These results imply that collaborative cognition expands exploration behavior but does not affect discriminative abilities of the attackers under uncertainty.

item.title: Beyond technology acceptance: students’ perceptions and prompt engineering competence in higher education
item.description:
Interactive Learning Environments
The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into Higher Education requires understanding students' perceptions and competence in interacting with these technologies. This mixed-methods study examined perceptions of GenAI and documented prompt engineering competence in academic tasks among 89 Psychology and Biomedical Engineering students. Study 1 employed a 2 × 2 quasi-experimental factorial design comparing disciplinary area and instructional approach (guided vs. autonomous), complemented by thematic analysis. Students reported favourable views of GenAI, particularly for understanding, learning, guidance, and work planning, while emphasising the need to verify AI-generated information and improve reliability and contextual accuracy. No significant multivariate effects of disciplinary area, instructional approach, or their interaction were found. However, item-level analyses identified two items with higher scores under autonomous instruction after multiple-comparison adjustment. Study 2 examined documented prompt engineering competence in 24 group reports using five rubric dimensions and the exploratory Prompt Competence Index (PCI). No differences between instructional approaches remained significant after multiple-comparison adjustment, although descriptive differences in Iteration and PCI emerged among biomedical engineering reports. Overall, findings support contextualised, iterative, and critically supervised human–AI interaction, while suggesting that instructional differences are context- and indicator-specific. Further validation of the PCI in larger, diverse, and balanced samples is required.

item.title: Leveraging generative AI for human understanding: meta-requirements and design principles for Explanatory AI as an emerging paradigm
item.description:
Behaviour and Information Technology
Artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly support decision-making across critical domains, yet explainable AI (XAI) approaches prioritise algorithmic transparency over human comprehension. While XAI reveals computational processes for model validation, end users require explanations integrating domain knowledge, contextual reasoning, and professional frameworks. This disconnect reveals a design challenge: existing approaches fail to address how practitioners need to understand and act upon AI recommendations. This paper introduces Explanatory AI as an emerging complementary paradigm where AI systems leverage generative and multimodal capabilities to serve as explanatory partners for human understanding. Unlike traditional XAI, which answers ‘How did the algorithm decide?’ for validation purposes, Explanatory AI addresses ‘Why does this make sense?’ for practitioners making informed decisions. Through theory-informed design, we synthesise multidisciplinary perspectives from cognitive science, communication research, and education with empirical evidence from healthcare and AI expert interviews. Our analysis identifies five dimensions distinguishing Explanatory AI from XAI: explanatory purpose, communication mode, epistemic stance, adaptivity, and cognitive design. We derive five meta-requirements and formulate ten design principles prescribing how to build such systems, illustrated through five UI mockups exemplifying implementation. Explanatory AI operates standalone or combined with XAI, serving distinct purposes in creating systems that genuinely support human reasoning and decision-making.

item.title: Taking a bottom–up, data-driven approach to characterizing variability across early-life environments.
item.description:
American Psychologist
Children's long-term outcomes correlate with the physical and social features of the homes, schools, and neighborhoods in which they grow up. Yet, current techniques for establishing these correlations are limited. This article (a) presents five main issues linked to the currently used approaches. For example, most research relies on questionnaires or coding brief videoed interactions, which focus on a limited set of dimensions selected by researchers ("top-down" approach). As a result, these methods are limited because they provide only a static snapshot, which often conflates conceptually diverse levels, including the physical (e.g., noise, light) and social environments (e.g., caregiver mood, responsiveness). New technologies offer alternative approaches to these issues. This article (b) highlights how continuous multifeature observations, processed using machine learning tools, can improve our description of early development and inform theorizing of the mechanisms through which environments shape outcomes. Devices worn by children and those around them provide long-form recordings, allowing researchers to track how naturalistic environments vary over time and how children respond to them in real time. This shift supports a more dynamic, bottom-up, data-driven, and potentially culturally neutral approach to characterizing environmental variability. Finally, the article (c) discusses key limitations, notably the need to ensure that machine learning methods used to analyze early environments are trained using culturally diverse data, evaluating remaining risks of bias, and practical and ethical considerations.
